profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a company building a cloud-based spreadsheet quality tool that recently added a 'calculation fragments' feature for testing and debugging complex spreadsheets. A pilot customer using a large financial planning workbook reported two linked problems: the tool sometimes takes over a minute to generate a fragment, and when a fragment is shown, the customer often marks it as 'correct' even though the underlying spreadsheet bug is still present. The agenda is to compare what each person has seen in logs and support artifacts, narrow down whether the real issue is fragment generation, fragment presentation, or the reproduction setup, and agree on a concrete next debugging step. The expected outcome is a shared plan for reproducing the issue and a candidate fix direction for the next patch.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: Spreadsheet dependency graphs, formula evaluation services, performance profiling
members.background: Priya built the service that extracts dependency-based calculation fragments from uploaded workbooks and recently optimized it for large models with many cross-sheet references and named ranges.
members.private_state: She wants to show that the core fragment algorithm is sound and suspects the problem is either in the reproduction workbook or in how the UI scopes what users are asked to validate; she is also trying to avoid a risky rewrite of the graph cache before the next release cut.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'fragment,' they mean the full dependency slice computed by the service, including off-screen named ranges, hidden sheets, and lookup chains, not just the cells visibly rendered in the panel.
The 'July repro workbook' everyone has been discussing is the sanitized support copy exported for engineering, which already removed external links and replaced some volatile formulas with values.
Saying the timeout is 'fixed' means the fragment-generation request stays under the backend SLA for the problematic workbook after caches are warm.
If the team agrees to 'make recomputation incremental,' that means persisting and reusing the workbook dependency graph across user interactions within the same session.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Customer incident triage, observability, end-to-end reproduction of spreadsheet tool failures
members.background: Leo handles pilot-customer escalations, watches session replays and traces, and has been replaying the customer issue using recorded uploads and the current staging build.
members.private_state: He wants a fix that makes the customer-facing debugging flow feel reliable in real sessions, and he is worried engineering is optimizing an internal service measure while missing what users actually see when validating a fragment.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'fragment,' they mean the reduced cell cluster the user can actually inspect in the UI without expanding advanced details, because that is what determines whether validation is manageable.
The 'July repro workbook' refers to the original pilot upload captured from production, which still contains external references, hidden tabs, and the exact formulas the customer saw.
Saying the timeout is 'fixed' means a pilot user can click into debugging and get a usable fragment quickly enough on a first attempt, without long preprocessing or repeated spinners.

If the team agrees to 'make recomputation incremental,' that means recalculating only the currently displayed fragment after each focus change, regardless of whether session-level graph caching exists.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the fragment' as the unit the user validates
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the backend-generated dependency slice, which may include hidden or collapsed cells, named ranges, and lookup tables that are part of the causal chain even if not visibly shown.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the visibly rendered subset of cells in the UI panel that the customer actually inspects when deciding whether the result looks correct.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing the same feature and the same screenshots, so 'fragment' feels like an obvious shared term; neither expects that the other is distinguishing between computed scope and visible scope.

misalignment_points.topic: Which workbook is the reproduction basis
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention 'the July repro workbook' or 'the customer workbook'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the sanitized engineering copy stored in S3, where external links were flattened and several volatile formulas were replaced to make profiling stable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the original production upload attached to the support ticket, including hidden sheets and live external-link formulas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The two files came from the same incident, have near-identical names, and were both circulated in the same Slack thread, so casual reference to 'the repro workbook' sounds fully specific enough.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to fix the timeout
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they need to 'fix the timeout' before the next pilot patch
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means fragment generation for the problematic workbook should complete within the service SLA after the workbook graph has already been loaded and cached.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first end-to-end user interaction in a debugging session should feel fast enough that the customer does not hit a spinner or abandon the validation flow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about performance in the same incident and using the same logs, so 'fix the timeout' sounds like a single operational goal even though one standard is backend-centric and the other is user-session-centric.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'incremental recompute' is the right next step
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means persisting the dependency graph and reusing it across navigation events and edits within one workbook session so the service avoids rebuilding lineage repeatedly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means recalculating only the currently displayed fragment on each focus change, even if the overall workbook graph is rebuilt each time in the background.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Incremental recompute is a familiar technical phrase that usually signals alignment; each assumes the other shares the default implementation pattern from their own layer of the system.

turns.inner_thought: The pilot complaint is really about the user flow, not just a backend number. In the original production upload from July, they click into debugging, stare at a spinner, then get a small fragment panel that looks tidy enough to approve even though the workbook output is still wrong. I need to anchor us on what the customer actually experienced with that exact customer workbook, not an engineering-friendly copy.
turns.utterance: I can start with the pilot summary. On the July repro workbook, the debugger still hangs long enough that the customer notices, and then when the fragment finally shows up they often mark it correct even though the underlying output is still wrong. So from my side it's both the delay and the fact that the fragment isn't helping them catch the bug.

turns.inner_thought: On the sanitized engineering repro in S3, fragment extraction itself is not the scary part once the dependency graph is loaded. My traces showed sub-30-second completion on the service path after warm cache, which is within the direction we wanted. I need to avoid the team concluding the graph layer is broken and pushing for a risky cache rewrite right before release.
turns.utterance: That matches some of what I've been looking at, but in my traces on the July repro workbook the fragment service itself is usually under thirty seconds once the graph is loaded. So I don't think the core extraction path is blowing up every time.

turns.inner_thought: Thirty seconds after the graph is loaded is not what the customer feels. In replay, first click is the issue: they wait through a long spinner before anything usable appears. And what appears is only the visible fragment panel, which is small enough that they assume it covers the relevant logic. I need to keep pulling the discussion back to first-attempt usability.
turns.utterance: Right, but in session replay the customer doesn't experience it as 'the service finished eventually.' They click in, see a long spinner, and during that whole time they have nothing to inspect. Then what they do get is a pretty small fragment panel. So from the user side we still haven't fixed the timeout.

turns.inner_thought: The fragment for that output isn't actually huge in dependency terms; it's mostly named ranges, hidden sheets, and lookup chains that the service correctly includes even if the panel doesn't render them all up front. That supports my suspicion that the algorithm is sound and the confusion may be in UI scoping or presentation, not lineage computation.
turns.utterance: One thing that may be making this feel stranger is that the fragment for the flagged output is actually pretty modest. A lot of the logic there isn't a giant visible cluster, so the fragment size by itself doesn't look like it should explain the wait.

turns.inner_thought: In the original customer workbook, the issue seems tied to a hidden assumptions tab plus an external FX reference that still fires when debugging starts. If Priya's numbers don't show that, she's probably looking at the sanitized copy, but both files have been called the July repro workbook for weeks. I won't derail us with file archaeology unless I need to.
turns.utterance: What I keep seeing on the customer workbook is that the bad case seems tied to a hidden assumptions tab and an external FX rate link that still lights up during the debugging flow. That's part of why I don't think we can treat this as just a big-but-normal fragment.

turns.inner_thought: That doesn't line up with the workbook I profiled at all; the sanitized engineering copy had external links removed and some volatile formulas flattened specifically so we could get stable traces. If Leo is seeing external-link behavior, he's almost certainly on a different artifact. Still, the safer framing is that whatever delay remains is probably cold-start preprocessing before first request, not fragment extraction. That keeps us away from a rewrite.
turns.utterance: Interesting. The workbook I profiled should not be paying that cost, which makes me think the remaining timeout is probably in preprocessing around the first request rather than in fragment extraction itself.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, maybe the delay is front-loaded. The product problem is still that users bounce between suspicious outputs and keep hitting waiting states. What I want is incremental recompute in the sense of only refreshing the currently displayed fragment each time they change focus, so the next click feels immediate even if deeper work continues elsewhere.
turns.utterance: Yeah, and for the next pilot patch I think the practical way to fix the timeout is incremental recompute. If a user moves from one suspicious result to the next, they shouldn't have to sit through the same long wait again.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that's exactly the direction I can support without ripping out the cache. Incremental recompute should mean we keep the workbook dependency graph alive within the session and reuse it across navigation events. That's a contained change and gives me a strong chance of meeting backend SLA after warmup.
turns.utterance: I agree. Incremental recompute should be pretty straightforward if we keep the workbook dependency graph alive for the rest of the debugging session. That ought to take a lot of repeated work out of the path.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the current panel refreshes quickly when focus changes, I don't really care whether the system keeps a graph alive or not. The customer's mental model is just 'I clicked another suspect value, show me that fragment now.' I should make sure that user-facing behavior is part of the plan.
turns.utterance: Exactly. From the customer side, the key thing is that switching focus should refresh only the currently shown fragment rather than making them wait on everything behind it. If that feels snappy, the flow becomes a lot more trustworthy.

turns.inner_thought: Before anyone commits to a UI or cache change, I want a clean measurement split on the sanitized repro workbook: cold graph build versus fragment-generation time. If the service path is already fine after warm cache, I can show the algorithm is sound and keep the patch targeted. Also, using the engineering copy avoids noisy external-link behavior.
turns.utterance: Before we lock in the patch shape, I'd like to do one quick experiment on the repro file: separate cold-start graph build time from fragment-generation time and see exactly where the delay sits. That should tell us whether we're fixing the right part of the stack.

turns.inner_thought: I'll rerun on staging with the original support artifact, because that's the only way I'll know whether the first user interaction is actually better. My success criterion is simple: when the same pilot flow starts, the fragment the user sees needs to become usable faster, not just produce cleaner service traces.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll rerun the July case on staging and use the same support artifact as before, then report back on whether the fragment becomes usable faster from the user's point of view.

turns.inner_thought: I'll prototype session-level graph reuse behind a flag, compare warm and cold timings on the engineering repro, and bring numbers to patch review. If I can show incremental recompute gets us under the service target after the first load, I can avoid a dangerous cache rewrite and argue the remaining issue is presentation or reproduction setup.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll prototype incremental recompute behind a flag and put timing comparisons together before patch review. If the numbers move the way I expect, we should have a concrete fix direction for the timeout.
